claim: Apidaecin (Api) is an 18-amino acid proline-rich antimicrobial peptide from honeybees.
source: Apidaecin is an 18-amino acid proline-rich antimicrobial peptide (PrAMP). Various PrAMPs are produced by insects and mammals to protect the host from bacterial infections (Graf and Wilson, 2019; Scocchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The text directly states the peptide length, type, and origin, with supporting citations.

claim: Apidaecin was described as the first antibiotic specifically targeting translation termination.
source: It was only recently that apidaecin, an antimicrobial peptide from honeybees (Casteels et al., 1989), was described as the first antibiotic specifically targeting translation termination (Florin et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with a citation to Florin et al., 2017.

claim: PrAMPs bind in the vacant nascent peptide exit tunnel of the large ribosomal subunit.
source: PrAMPs bind in the vacant nascent peptide exit tunnel of the large ribosomal subunit (Gagnon et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2015; Seefeldt et al., 2016; Seefeldt et al., 2015).
evidence: The text directly states the binding location with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Most PrAMPs invade the peptidyl transferase center and arrest the ribosome at the start codon by hindering the binding of the first elongator aminoacyl-tRNA.
source: Most of the PrAMPs described to date invade the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) and by hindering the binding of the first elongator aminoacyl-tRNA, arrest the ribosome at the start codon (Gagnon et al., 2016; Seefeldt et al., 2016).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Apidaecin does not directly obstruct the catalytic site of the ribosome despite binding in the exit tunnel and approaching the PTC.
source: Even though this PrAMP also binds in the exit tunnel and closely approaches the PTC, it does not directly obstruct the catalytic site (Florin et al., 2017; Krizsan et al., 2015).
evidence: The text explicitly states this distinction with citations.

claim: Api traps deacyl-tRNA in the P site and class one release factors (RF1 or RF2) in the A site.
source: Biochemical analyses carried out with the synthetic peptide Api137 (Berthold et al., 2013; referred to, throughout, as Api) showed that Api traps deacyl-tRNA in the P site and class one release factors (RF1 or RF2) in the A site.
evidence: The text directly states the biochemical findings with citations.

claim: Api can bind only after the ribosome has reached the stop codon, associated with RF1/RF2, and released the fully-synthesized protein.
source: The model that emerged from these in vitro studies (Florin et al., 2017) postulated that Api can bind only after the ribosome has reached the stop codon, associated with RF1/RF2, and released the fully-synthesized protein, because only then the exit tunnel becomes available for Api binding.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the proposed model with citation.

claim: Addition of Api to a cell-free translation system can lead to the accumulation of unhydrolyzed peptidyl-tRNA.
source: Strikingly, however, addition of Api to a cell-free translation system could also lead to the accumulation of unhydrolyzed peptidyl-tRNA, indicating that Api is also able to interfere with peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis at stop codons (Florin et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation with citation.

claim: Translation of a GFP reporter protein was significantly inhibited by Api in bacterial cells, whereas expression of the same reporter in a cell-free system was only marginally affected even at high Api concentrations.
source: Furthermore, there is a seeming discrepancy regarding the in vitro and in vivo modes of Api action, since the translation of a GFP reporter protein was significantly inhibited by Api in bacterial cells, whereas expression of the same reporter in a cell-free system was only marginally affected even at high Api concentrations (Krizsan et al., 2015; Krizsan et al., 2014).
evidence: The text explicitly describes this discrepancy with citations.

claim: Incubation of E. coli cultures for 1 min with 1.25 µM of Api (MIC) reduced translation by as much as 75%.
source: Exposure to 1.25 µM of Api, which corresponds to the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) that prevents cell growth, reduced translation by as much as 75%.
evidence: The text directly states the experimental result.

claim: Treatment for 2 min with 4× MIC of Api diminished protein synthesis to nearly 10% of the control.
source: Treatment for 2 min with 4× MIC diminished protein synthesis to nearly 10% of the control and extending the treatment to 10 min achieved ~94% inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text states the result with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: Exposure to Api caused a dramatic redistribution of ribosomes along mRNAs with a buildup of ribosome density toward the ends of the ORFs.
source: Exposure to Api caused a dramatic redistribution of ribosomes along mRNAs. The general pattern observed within individual genes revealed a buildup of ribosome density toward the ends of the ORFs, often spilling into the 3'-intergenic regions (Figure 1A, Source data 1).
evidence: The text describes the observation with reference to figure data.

claim: Api treatment results in a significant (~tenfold) increase of the average normalized ribosome density at stop codons.
source: A prominent outcome of Api treatment is a significant (~tenfold) increase of the average normalized ribosome density at stop codons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the quantitative finding with figure reference.

claim: Approximately 11% of all the ribosome footprints in Api-exposed cells map to stop codons.
source: Approximately 11% of all the ribosome footprints in Api-exposed cells map to stop codons.
evidence: The text directly states this quantitative result.

claim: Api acts as a potent global inhibitor of translation termination in bacterial cells.
source: This result reveals Api as a potent global inhibitor of translation termination in bacterial cells and expands the previous findings of the in vitro experiments which showed that Api could arrest ribosomes at the stop codon of several model genes during cell-free translation (Florin et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the data and prior work.

claim: In Api-treated cells, 97% of genes showed SC scores that shifted to higher values compared to the untreated control.
source: In the Api-treated cells, the SC scores of 97% of genes shifted to higher values compared to the untreated control.
evidence: The text directly states this quantitative result.

claim: More than half (56%) of the genes in the Api sample exhibited SC scores above 8 (log2 = 3).
source: Although SC scores varied significantly between the genes, more than half (56%) of the genes in the Api sample exhibited values above 8 (log2 = 3), whereas only 1% of the genes in the control cells showed such high scores, reflecting the dramatic increase in stop codon occupancy caused by Api (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this quantitative finding with figure reference.

claim: Api efficiently acts upon both class 1 release factors (RF1 and RF2).
source: This result shows that Api efficiently acts upon both class 1 RFs, thereby contradicting a recent suggestion that Api preferentially traps RF1 over RF2 (Kuru et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the data and contrasts it with another study.

claim: pLogo analysis showed statistically significant prevalence of glycine residues at the C-termini of proteins encoded in ORFs with high SC-scores.
source: The pLogo analysis showed statistically significant prevalence of glycine residues at the C-termini of such proteins, a tendency not observed in high SC-scoring ORFs in the untreated cells.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from the analysis.

claim: At least three distinct waves of ribosome density are observed in the metagene profile upstream from the stop codons in the Api sample.
source: At least three distinct waves of ribosome density are observed in the metagene profile upstream from the stop codons in the Api sample (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly describes this observation with figure reference.

claim: The crests of the ribosome density waves are spaced by ~27 nt, a distance corresponding to the peak of the footprint length distribution.
source: The crests of the waves are spaced by ~27 nt, a distance corresponding to the peak of the footprint length distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this upstream density likely represents elongating ribosomes queued behind those arrested at stop codons.
evidence: The text explicitly states this measurement with figure reference and interpretation.

claim: The upstream ribosome density likely represents elongating ribosomes queued behind those arrested at stop codons.
source: The crests of the waves are spaced by ~27 nt, a distance corresponding to the peak of the footprint length distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this upstream density likely represents elongating ribosomes queued behind those arrested at stop codons.
evidence: The text explicitly provides this interpretation based on the data.

claim: In the Api sample, 90% of the genes have an RT score greater than 1, indicating higher relative density in the 3'UTR than in the ORF itself.
source: In contrast, in the Api sample, 90% of the genes have an RT score greater than 1, indicating higher relative density in the 3'UTR than in the ORF itself due to pervasive and efficient stop codon bypass (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this quantitative finding with figure references.

claim: All stop codons are bypassed with comparable efficiency in Api-treated cells.
source: We found no strong correlation between the stop codon identity and the RT score, indicating that all the stop codons are bypassed with comparable efficiency in the Api-treated cells, in contrast to the control cells, where UAA genes have significantly lower RT scores (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the data analysis.

claim: The ribosome-depleted lysates of Api-treated cells essentially lacked free RF2.
source: Strikingly, unlike those of the control sample, the ribosome-depleted lysates of Api-treated cells essentially lacked free RF2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation with figure reference.

claim: Metagene analysis shows a peak of ribosome footprints at the first in-frame downstream stop codon.
source: Indeed, metagene analysis shows a peak of ribosome footprints at the first in-frame downstream stop codon (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), indicating that ribosomes that bypassed the termination signal of the main ORF are actively translating downstream mRNA sequences.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure reference and interpretation.

claim: A significant number of peptides encoded in the genomic regions downstream from the ORF stop codons were identified in Api-treated samples but not in control samples.
source: Even when applying strict filtering criteria (Gessulat et al., 2019), we were able to identify a significant number of peptides encoded in the genomic regions downstream from the ORF stop codons in both of the Api samples (Figure 4B and Source data 3). The same analysis found no such peptides in the control sample.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure and data references.

claim: Approximately half (49%) of the identified 'extension' peptides were encoded in frame with the upstream ORF.
source: Approximately half (49%) of the identified 'extension' peptides were encoded in frame with the upstream ORF (Figure 4C) and thus, were likely produced by the ribosomes that misread the main ORF stop codon as a sense codon and continued translating the downstream mRNA sequence.
evidence: The text explicitly states this quantitative finding with figure reference and interpretation.

claim: In three identified tryptic peptides encoded in mRNA sequences spanning the ORF termination signal, the stop codon was mistranslated by a near-cognate aminoacyl-tRNA.
source: Consistently, in the three identified tryptic peptides encoded in mRNA sequences spanning the ORF termination signal, the stop codon was mistranslated by a near-cognate aminoacyl-tRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure reference.

claim: Puromycin treatment of lysate from Api-treated cells significantly reduced the relative amounts of queued ribosomes and 3'UTR ribosomes.
source: Indeed, metagene analysis showed that Pmn treatment of lysate from Api-treated cells significantly reduced the relative amounts of queued ribosomes and 3'UTR ribosomes and, consequently, increased the relative occupancy of stop codons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure reference.

claim: Among the top 50 proteins whose abundance is increased in cells exposed to 0.5× MIC of Api, 19 are related to translation.
source: Among the top 50 proteins whose abundance is increased in the cells exposed to 0.5× MIC of Api, 19 are related to translation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure reference.

claim: The highest peak of ribosome occupancy in Api-treated cells corresponds to the stop codon of the degron-encoding sequence in tmRNA.
source: Analysis of the Ribo-seq data showed that the highest peak of ribosome occupancy in the Api-treated cells corresponds to the stop codon of the degron-encoding sequence in tmRNA (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure references.

claim: tmRNA is a component of a conserved bacterial system that rescues stalled mRNA-associated ribosomes with an empty A site.
source: tmRNA is a component of a conserved bacterial system that rescues stalled mRNA-associated ribosomes with an empty A site (Buskirk and Green, 2017; Moore and Sauer, 2005).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with citations.

claim: For the arfA gene in Api-treated cells, there was a nearly tenfold increase in the abundance of its transcript and a more than sevenfold higher number of ribosomes associated with its mRNA.
source: For the arfA gene in the Api-treated cells, we observed a nearly tenfold increase in the abundance of its transcript and a more than sevenfold higher number of ribosomes associated with its mRNA (Figure 5D and Source datas 5 and 6).
evidence: The text explicitly states these quantitative findings with figure and data references.

claim: The relative amount of arfB transcripts increases by ~40% and there are ~4 times more ribosomes per arfB transcript in Api-treated cells.
source: The relative amount of arfB transcripts increases by ~40% and there are ~4 times more ribosomes per arfB transcript (Source datas 5 and 6).
evidence: The text explicitly states these quantitative findings with data references.

claim: Deletion of tmRNA, arfA, or arfB genes does not increase cell sensitivity to Api.
source: Consistently, deletion of tmRNA, arfA, or arfB genes does not increase cell sensitivity to Api (Source data 7).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with data reference.

claim: A metagene analysis of the 5' ends of genes showed a moderate increase (~twofold) of the number of ribosome footprints at the start codons of the ORFs in the Api sample compared to the control.
source: While the predominant effect of Api on cellular translation is the build-up of ribosome density in the vicinity of stop codons (Figure 2A), a metagene analysis of the 5' ends of genes showed a moderate increase (~twofold) of the number of ribosome footprints at the start codons of the ORFs in the Api sample compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure references.

claim: Increasing Api concentration to 2 mM led to the appearance of start codon toeprint bands in the zntA and tyrS templates.
source: However, increasing Api concentration to 2 mM led to the appearance of a start codon toeprint bands in the zntA and tyrS templates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–C); the start codon effects were much weaker or completely absent with the other tested genes.
evidence: The text explicitly states this experimental finding with figure references.

claim: A larger fraction of the ribosomes associated with stop codons is likely arrested in a post-release state, with Api bound in the exit tunnel, trapped RF1 or RF2 in the A site, and deacylated tRNA in the P site.
source: A larger fraction of the ribosomes associated with stop codons is likely arrested in a post-release state, with Api bound in the exit tunnel, trapped RF1 or RF2 in the A site, and deacylated tRNA in the P site.
evidence: The text explicitly states this interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Most of the available RFs are sequestered in Api-stalled ribosome complexes.
source: Most of the available RFs are sequestered in these complexes (Figure 2B), which explains why overexpression of class 1 RFs reduced the sensitivity of E. coli to Api (Matsumoto et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with figure reference and citation.

claim: The number of ribosomes in the cell exceeds the copy number of RF1 and RF2.
source: In normal conditions, however, because the number of ribosomes in the cell exceeds the copy number of RF1 and RF2 (Schmidt et al., 2016), some ribosomes likely become stalled at stop codons in a pre-release state, with a vacant A site and the completed protein still esterifying P-site tRNA.
evidence: The text explicitly states this with citation.

claim: The number of the total stop codon footprints (~11% of all mapped footprints) roughly matches the ratio between ribosomes and RFs in the cell.
source: However, because the number of the total stop codon footprints (~11% of all mapped footprints) roughly matches the ratio between ribosomes and RFs in the cell (Schmidt et al., 2016), it is likely that most of the ribosome density detected at stop codons is accounted for by Api-stalled post-release ribosomes.
evidence: The text explicitly states this comparison with citation.

claim: Api-induced ribosome stalling at stop codons causes severe ribosome queuing.
source: Api-induced ribosome stalling at stop codons causes severe ribosome queuing.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Api needs to bind to only a few terminating ribosomes to preclude a much larger number of inhibitor-free ribosomes from participating in translation.
source: The pronounced ribosome queuing in the Api-treated cells illustrates a distinctive feature of a translation termination inhibitor as an antimicrobial: Api needs to bind to only a few terminating ribosomes to preclude a much larger number of inhibitor-free ribosomes from participating in translation.
evidence: The text explicitly states this interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Termination arrest and ribosome queuing did not increase the number of heavy polysomes in the cell.
source: Termination arrest and ribosome queuing, however, did not increase the number of heavy polysomes in the cell, likely because in fast-growing cells ~90% of the ribosomes are already associated with mRNAs (Bartholomäus et al., 2016; Bremer and Dennis, 1996) and thus, blocking termination would not perceptibly increase ribosome loading per mRNA.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with citations and interpretation.

claim: Stop codon bypass is likely a consequence of the Api-mediated depletion of available RFs that increases the residence time of pre-release state ribosomes at the stop codons of the ORFs.
source: Stop codon bypass is likely a consequence of the Api-mediated depletion of available RFs (Figure 2B) that increases the residence time of pre-release state ribosomes at the stop codons of the ORFs, leading ultimately to readthrough.
evidence: The text explicitly states this mechanistic interpretation with figure reference.

claim: Api's ability to stimulate bypass appears to be more robust than aminoglycosides, odilorhabdins, or negamycin, leading to the appearance of ribosome footprints downstream of not only the first but also of the subsequent stop codons.
source: However, Api's ability to stimulate bypass appears to be more robust, leading to the appearance of ribosome footprints downstream of not only the first but also of the subsequent stop codons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this comparison with figure reference.

claim: Unlike miscoding antibiotics, Api does not reduce the general accuracy of translation.
source: Additionally, unlike miscoding antibiotics, Api does not reduce the general accuracy of translation and thus, could be exploited for medical applications where a premature stop codon readthrough is desirable (Huang et al., 2019; Keeling et al., 2014).
evidence: The text explicitly states this distinction with citations.

claim: Api-induced stop codon bypass is achieved by either misincorporation of a near-cognate amino acid at the stop codon or via (−1) or (+1) frameshifting.
source: Api-induced stop codon bypass is achieved by either misincorporation of a near-cognate amino acid at the stop codon or via (−1) or (+1) frameshifting leading to the synthesis of proteins with C-terminal extensions.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the data.

claim: Under Api treatment conditions, no significant accumulation of protein aggregates was detected.
source: Although under our Api treatment conditions, we did not detect any significant accumulation of protein aggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), it remains possible that accumulation of proteins with C-terminal appendages could contribute to the antimicrobial activity of Api since these aberrant extensions may negatively affect the proteins' catalytic capacity, ligand binding, or interactions with other polypeptides.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with figure reference.

claim: By allowing translation to proceed to the 3' ends of mRNA transcripts and by prompting some of the translating ribosomes to stall at the stop codons in a pre-release state, Api triggers the activation of the ribosome rescue systems.
source: By allowing translation to proceed to the 3' ends of mRNA transcripts (Figure 5C,D) and by prompting some of the translating ribosomes to stall at the stop codons in a pre-release state, Api triggers the activation of the ribosome rescue systems.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion with figure references.

claim: The lack of available RF1/RF2 in Api-treated cells prevents the release of the degron-tagged protein, thereby sequestering tmRNA.
source: Yet, the lack of available RF1/RF2 in the Api-treated cells prevents the release of the degron-tagged protein, therefore sequestering tmRNA.
evidence: The text explicitly states this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The depletion of the available tmRNA pool leads to activation of the backup rescue systems.
source: The depletion of the available tmRNA pool leads to activation of the backup rescue systems, which nevertheless, should be also ineffectual in the Api-treated cells.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: The lack of available RF2 in Api-treated cells should prevent ArfA from carrying out its rescue mission.
source: Once again, the lack of available RF2 in the Api-treated cells should prevent ArfA from carrying out its rescue mission.
evidence: The text explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: Api can trap ArfB on the ribosome and deplete its available pool.
source: Despite acting independently from the primary RFs, the alternative RF ArfB, should be equally inconsequential because Api can also trap ArfB on the ribosome (Chan et al., 2020) and deplete its available pool.
evidence: The text explicitly states this with citation.

claim: None of the known ways that the bacterial cell normally exploits for salvaging stalled ribosomes would be of much use when translation is inhibited by Api.
source: Thus, it appears that none of the known ways that the bacterial cell normally exploits for salvaging stalled ribosomes would be of much use when the translation is inhibited by Api.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: The inactivation of any of the rescue systems does not sensitize E. coli to the Api action.
source: In agreement with this notion, the inactivation of any of the rescue systems does not sensitize E. coli to the Api action (Source data 7).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with data reference.

claim: The increased ribosome occupancy of start codons of some genes could be related to the reported low affinity of Api for the ribosome with the vacant nascent peptide exit tunnel.
source: One of the unexpected aspects of Api action revealed by the in vivo studies is the increased ribosome occupancy of start codons of some genes. These effects could be related to the reported low affinity of Api for the ribosome with the vacant nascent peptide exit tunnel (Florin et al., 2017; Kolano et al., 2020; Krizsan et al., 2014).
evidence: The text explicitly states this interpretation with citations.

claim: Exposure of cells to Api leads to translation arrest at stop codons of multiple ORFs, ribosome queuing and depletion of available RFs resulting in a rapid halt of protein synthesis.
source: Exposure of cells to Api, leads to translation arrest at stop codons of multiple ORFs, ribosome queuing and depletion of available RFs resulting in a rapid halt of protein synthesis.
evidence: The text explicitly states this summary of the mechanism.

claim: In cell-free systems where only one type of mRNA is present, many mRNA molecules will be translated at least once before the Api-induced depletion of the RF pool, thereby resulting in poor inhibition of the reporter expression.
source: By contrast, in cell-free systems, where only one type of mRNA is present, many mRNA molecules will be translated at least once before the Api-induced depletion of the RF pool, thereby resulting in poor inhibition of the reporter expression.
evidence: The text explicitly states this explanation for the in vitro/in vivo discrepancy.

claim: The use of Ribo-seq in combination with retapamulin was instrumental in identifying translation start sites in bacteria, revealing a universe of cryptic protein-coding sequences.
source: The use of Ribo-seq in combination with the translation initiation inhibitor retapamulin was instrumental in identifying translation start sites in bacteria, revealing a universe of cryptic protein-coding sequences (Meydan et al., 2019; Weaver et al., 2019).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with citations.

claim: Ribo-seq enhanced by the use of a translation termination inhibitor could bolster our ability to detect the translated sequences in the bacterial genomes.
source: Ribo-seq, enhanced by the use of a translation termination inhibitor, could bolster our ability to detect the translated sequences in the bacterial genomes.
evidence: The text explicitly states this potential application.

claim: The effects of Api are multifaceted and lead not only to translation arrest at the stop codons but also to ribosome queuing and stop codon readthrough.
source: Because the effects of Api are multifaceted and lead not only to translation arrest at the stop codons but also to ribosome queuing and stop codon readthrough (Figure 2A), its immediate application for mapping translation termination sites could be challenging.
evidence: The text explicitly states this summary with figure reference.

claim: With properly optimized Pmn treatment to remove queued and elongating ribosomes, Api could be repurposed for genome-wide analysis of stop codons of protein-coding regions.
source: Nevertheless, with additional tricks, for example, properly optimized Pmn treatment to remove queued and elongating ribosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), Api could be repurposed for genome-wide analysis of stop codons of protein-coding regions.
evidence: The text explicitly states this potential application with figure reference.

claim: The use of Ribo-seq in combination with inhibitors of translation initiation and termination could provide new insights into the principles of genetic encoding and regulation of gene expression.
source: The use of Ribo-seq in combination with inhibitors of translation initiation and termination could provide new insights into the principles of genetic encoding and regulation of gene expression.
evidence: The text explicitly states this potential application.
